section_summary: This section of Record Group 59 (decimal file 894.00) covers Japanese domestic political affairs from early 1930 through late 1931, focusing on the aftermath of the 1930 general election, the lifting of the gold embargo, and the political reverberations of the London Naval Treaty. It documents court indictments of former cabinet ministers in railway bribery scandals, progressive attempts to reform internal procedure in the Privy Council against the dominance of Count Miyoji Ito, and the consolidation of proletarian parties into the National Popular Party. Crucially, the section details the political crisis and succession maneuvering triggered by the wounding of Prime Minister Yuko Hamaguchi, leading to the formation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and clashes between the government, press, and military. Later documents trace escalating civil-military tensions following the September 1931 Mukden Incident, including rumored coup attempts, officer detentions, and Foreign Minister Shidehara's embattled efforts to negotiate troop withdrawal principles amidst rising militarism.

subfiles.about: Continues an in-depth analysis of the February 1930 Japanese general election, evaluating voter turnout, campaign strategies, and party fortunes.
subfiles.summary: Evaluates the results of Japan's second general election under universal manhood suffrage, noting the decisive absolute majority achieved by the Minseito. Analyzes how party discipline under Adachi Kenzo and retrenchment economic policies contrasted with Seiyukai factional dissension between Suzuki and Tokonami followers. Highlights the unprecedented defeat of independent and minor-party candidates, the poor showing of fragmented proletarian groups, and prospects for establishing a genuine two-party system.
subfiles.title: Despatch on the Japanese General Election of 1930 (Continuation)

subfiles.about: Reports that preliminary court judges have indicted several former cabinet ministers and officials in railway bribery scandals and committed them to public trial.
subfiles.summary: Despatch: Japan indicts former ministers Kobashi, Ogawa, and ex-Chosen Governor-General Yamanashi, with twenty-eight others, in bribery scandals.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 114: Indictments in Government Bribery Scandals

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 150 regarding political unrest in Japan over the London Naval Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Neville's despatch reviews Japanese political unrest over the London Naval Treaty.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Despatch No. 150 regarding Political Unrest over the London Naval Treaty

subfiles.about: Reports the amalgamation of three proletarian parties into the National Popular Party (Zenkoku Taishu-to), enclosing its platform and party chart.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the Japan Popular Party, the National Democratic Party, and the Labor-Farmer Popular Party have merged to establish the National Popular Party (Zenkoku Taishu-to), reducing the number of proletarian parties from five to three. Analyzes the leadership and ideological stance of the new party, positioned between the conservative Social Democratic Party and the radical Labor-Farmer Party, while noting that personal rivalries among labor leaders often undermine unity. Transmits two enclosures detailing the sixteen chief principles of the new party and a schematic chart of Japanese proletarian political parties and their supporting labor federations.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 216: Amalgamation of Proletarian Parties into the National Popular Party

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing report No. 20 regarding the opening of judicial trials of public officials for corruption, focusing on General Yamanashi.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Forbes's report covers corruption trials of officials, with ex-Governor-General Yamanashi the central defendant.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Report No. 20 regarding Corruption Trials of Public Officials

subfiles.about: Summarizes political instability, economic distress, and cabinet succession rivalries following the attempted assassination of Prime Minister Hamaguchi.
subfiles.summary: Summary: Hamaguchi's slow recovery from shooting strains Minseito unity amid economic depression, with Shidehara acting premier and a Seiyuhonto push for Ugaki.
subfiles.title: Summary of Political Conditions and Cabinet Succession following Hamaguchi's Wounding

subfiles.about: Internal State Department minute evaluating Tokyo Despatch No. 33 regarding the powers and procedural reform of the Japanese Privy Council.
subfiles.summary: Minute praises the Embassy's review of Japan's Privy Council reforms, routing it to Western European Affairs.
subfiles.title: Department of State Minute on Privy Council Report

subfiles.about: Analyzes an unsuccessful movement by progressive members to reform the procedure and curb the autocratic political dominance of Count Ito in the Privy Council.
subfiles.summary: Examines efforts by progressive Privy Councillors led by Ryohei Okada to alter Council regulations following disputes over the London Naval Treaty, aiming to break the behind-the-scenes dominance of Count Miyoji Ito. Traces the Council's constitutional evolution since 1889 and explains how under Prince Yamagata it usurped extra-constitutional authority over cabinet policy, causing the fall of the Wakatsuki Cabinet in 1927. Concludes that while moderate and neutral members shelved formal procedural changes to avoid a crisis of confidence in President Kuratomi, councillors were ultimately permitted to attend committee hearings.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 33: Attempted Reforms and Political Role of the Japanese Privy Council

subfiles.about: Reports on Premier Hamaguchi's convalescence and the factional intrigues and economic pressures facing the Minseito government prior to the Diet session.
subfiles.summary: Informs the Department that while Prime Minister Hamaguchi is out of danger following his wounding, his prolonged hospitalization will prevent him from directing the government in the Diet. Discusses simmering intra-party rivalry between Adachi Kenzo and Egi Tasuku, alongside intense public dissatisfaction caused by agricultural depression, collapsing silk prices, and high urban unemployment. Outlines Baron Shidehara's desire to surrender the acting premiership before the session and analyzes moves by Seiyuhonto members to draft War Minister General Ugaki as interim premier.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 68: Political Complications Arising from Premier Hamaguchi's Disability

subfiles.about: Reports on persistent political unrest and factional maneuvering within the Minseito over government leadership during Hamaguchi's absence.
subfiles.summary: Despatch: Minseito elders back Hamaguchi's mandate despite his disability, as Shidehara reluctantly continues as premier amid friction over Adachi's liaison role.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 86: Intra-Party Discord over Interim Leadership of the Japanese Government

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 96 regarding freedom of the press in Japan and the detention of a newspaper reporter.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Forbes's despatch covers Japanese press freedom after a journalist's police detention.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Despatch No. 96 regarding Freedom of the Press in Japan

subfiles.about: Details the police detention of a Jiji Shimpo reporter, the united protest of Tokyo newspapers, and the resulting political embarrassment for Home Minister Adachi.
subfiles.summary: Reports on the arrest and four-day detention of a Jiji Shimpo reporter by the Tokyo police under Chief Maruyama, ostensibly for spreading rumors about Premier Hamaguchi's health but actually to spy on War Minister Ugaki's political plans. Describes how metropolitan newspapers united to pass a scathing resolution impeaching the government for press suppression, winning support from General Ugaki and the Privy Council. Explains how this uproar forced Home Minister Adachi to submit a formal written apology promising future respect for press freedom and punishment of responsible subordinates.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 96: Police Interference with the Press and Resulting Political Crisis

subfiles.about: Reports the en bloc resignation of the Hamaguchi Cabinet due to the Prime Minister's ill health and the impending appointment of Wakatsuki.
subfiles.summary: Telegram: Hamaguchi's cabinet resigns en bloc over his health; Wakatsuki asked to form a new government.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 50: En Bloc Resignation of the Hamaguchi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports the formation of a new Minseito cabinet by Baron Wakatsuki, noting ministerial continuity and no anticipated change in policy.
subfiles.summary: Telegram: Wakatsuki forms a new cabinet retaining Shidehara and Inouye, predicting continuity in Minseito policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 55: Formation of New Cabinet by Baron Wakatsuki

subfiles.about: Reports on Baron Wakatsuki's selection as Prime Minister following Hamaguchi's resignation, transmitting biographic profiles of three newly appointed cabinet ministers.
subfiles.summary: Details the events leading to the en bloc resignation of the Hamaguchi Cabinet after the Prime Minister required another operation, and the compromise selection of Baron Reijiro Wakatsuki to prevent disruption between Adachi Kenzo and Ugaki Kazushige. Analyzes Wakatsuki's public statements affirming financial retrenchment and the no-loan policy, and reviews press commentary on the new ministry. Encloses detailed confidential biographic data sheets for the three new cabinet appointees: War Minister General Jiro Minami, Overseas Affairs Minister Shujiro Hara, and Commerce and Industry Minister Yukio Sakurauchi.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 210: Organization of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and Biographic Profiles of New Ministers

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a confidential memorandum of conversation between Secretary Stimson and Ambassador Debuchi regarding Wakatsuki's retrenchment policy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Stimson and Ambassador Debuchi discussed Wakatsuki's fiscal retrenchment policy.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Memorandum of Conversation regarding Wakatsuki's Retrenchment Policy

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a Geneva telegram citing Yotaro Sugimura on the internal struggle between Japanese civil and military authorities.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Gilbert reports Tokyo's civil-military rift after the Mukden Incident as a fight to the death.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Geneva Telegram No. 129 regarding Tokyo Civil-Military Rift after Mukden Incident

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Political Report No. 45 concerning War Minister Minami's speech on Manchuria and Eugene Chen's departure from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Neville's report covers Minami's disarmament speech and Eugene Chen's Japan visit.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Political Report No. 45 regarding War Minister Minami's Speech and Eugene Chen's Visit

subfiles.about: Extracted pages from Political Report No. 45 detailing War Minister Minami's imperialistic speech and Eugene Chen's mysterious mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Extract: Minami's speech against disarmament angered Minseito, while Chen's secret Japan visit drew refused deportation demands and criticism of US arms sales.
subfiles.title: Extracts from Political Report No. 45 regarding War Minister Minami's Speech and Eugene Chen's Visit

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing confidential Telegram No. 191 concerning domestic political tension and suspected military coup plots.
subfiles.summary: Files Tokyo Telegram No. 191 under 793.94/2247, on Manchuria agitation, army officers' arrests, press censorship and Shidehara's statements.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Telegram No. 191 regarding Domestic Crisis and Coup Rumors

subfiles.about: Duplicate cross-reference sheet bearing file stamp 894.00/314 indexing Telegram No. 191 regarding domestic unrest and military coup rumors.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate Document File Note for Telegram No. 191, filed 894.00/314; original is under 793.94/2247.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Telegram No. 191 (Duplicate Copy)

subfiles.about: Reports severe domestic tension over Manchurian policy, the detention of army officers in gendarmerie headquarters over coup fears, and press censorship.
subfiles.summary: Reports government preoccupied with opposition to its Manchurian policy; army officers arrested at Gendarmerie Headquarters (October Incident); strict press censorship. Shidehara downplays civilian involvement and rumors.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 191: Domestic Unrest, Military Coup Rumors, and Officer Arrests

subfiles.about: Reports the results of prefectural assembly elections held across thirty-seven prefectures, highlighting a major victory for the Minseito.
subfiles.summary: Details the results of elections held on October 16, 1931, across thirty-seven prefectures, where the governing Minseito won an overwhelming victory, securing 802 seats and majorities in twenty-five prefectures compared to 635 seats for the Seiyukai. Attributes this success to the organizational skills of Home Minister Adachi and a public desire for national stability during the Manchurian crisis, despite widespread criticisms of Shidehara's foreign policy. Highlights the sharp decline of proletarian parties and the near-disappearance of neutral and minority political factions in local assemblies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 370: Results and Significance of the 1931 Prefectural Assembly Elections

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Telegram No. 209 concerning fears that militant elements may oust moderates from the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Telegram No. 209 (793.94/2498) from Ambassador Forbes: militant factions threaten to oust moderate statesmen amid opposition to Shidehara's policies.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Telegram No. 209 regarding Danger of Military Domination of Government

subfiles.about: Reports on a meeting with Foreign Minister Shidehara outlining Japan's five basic principles for troop withdrawal and warns of militant ascendancy.
subfiles.summary: Forbes interviews Shidehara on Japan's five principles for troop withdrawal in Manchuria, warning against agreements under military occupation. Embassy officers fear militants may overthrow the moderate government.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 209: Shidehara Interview on Five Principles for Troop Withdrawal and Political Crisis
